Insight1.summary: In aged female and male mice, senescence and DAM gene expression was more pronounced in fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum white matter than in hippocampal gray matter. Age-dependent increases in these transcriptional signatures were observed more consistently in white matter than in the hippocampus or cerebellum, emphasizing white matter susceptibility to late-life senescence and DAM changes.
Insight1.how: The authors compared RT-PCR measurements from microdissected fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum white matter with hippocampal gray matter in aged female and male mice. Several senescence and DAM-related genes were significantly higher in white matter, with additional female- or male-specific changes among particular transcripts. Comparisons with young, sex-matched mice showed that some genes increased in both gray and white matter, whereas a broader set increased in aged white matter, and the regional heat map showed more consistent age-related increases in white matter than in hippocampus or cerebellum. These findings support regional susceptibility of white matter to late-life transcriptional changes, but do not by themselves establish a mechanistically selective vulnerability.
Insight1.relevant: We investigated senescence and microglial gene expression patterns in microdissected fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum white matter relative to hippocampal gray matter of aged female and male mice (Fig. 1). p16ink4a (Fig. 1a), Cdkn2a (Fig. 1b), Lgals3 (Fig. 1c), Cdkn1a/p21 (Fig. 1d) and Ccl2 (Fig. 1e) expression were significantly higher in fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum compared with hippocampus. In aged female mice, Ccl5 (Fig. 1f), Apoe (Fig. 1g) and Gpr34 (Fig. 1h) expression were significantly higher in fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum compared with hippocampus. Relative to young counterparts, p16ink4a, Cdkn2a, Csf1r, Gpr34 and Trem2 expression increased in both gray and white matter microdissections of old male and female mice (Fig. 1i,j). Apoe, Bcl2a1a, Cd11b, Klk8, Lgals3, Cdkn1a/p21 and Tmem173 expression increased in old female and male fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum. Ccl2, Ccl5, Il1b and Tyrobp increased in old male fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum (Fig. 1j). In aged female and male mice, senescence and DAM gene expression was more pronounced in white matter relative to hippocampal gray matter. At the regional level, we observed age-dependent increases in genes such as p16ink4a, Cdkn2a, Lgals3, Apoe, Bcl2a1a, Cd11b, Csf1r, Klk8, Tmem173, Trem2 and Tyrobp more consistently in old fimbria-fornix and corpus callosum (Fig. 1k) than in the hippocampus or cerebellum, emphasizing that white matter is susceptible to late-life changes in senescence and DAM transcriptional signatures.

Insight2.summary: GAL3+ cells are rare in young mouse brains but accumulate densely in aged white matter tracts, especially the fimbria, where GAL3 colocalizes with IBA1 rather than GFAP. In aged female fimbria, IBA1+GAL3+ cells are larger than IBA1+GAL3− cells and show higher or trending-higher levels of uPAR and CD38; the age-associated increase in GAL3 area is more pronounced in females, while dPP4 elevation was demonstrated only for fimbria myeloid cells overall.
Insight2.how: Immunofluorescence mapped GAL3 in young and aged brains and used IBA1 and GFAP costaining to establish its association with myeloid rather than astrocytic cells in the fimbria. Sex-stratified measurements showed greater GAL3-positive area in old versus young female fimbria, whereas the corresponding male comparison was not significant. Morphological analysis found that IBA1+GAL3+ cells were larger than IBA1+GAL3− cells in old female fimbria, and PCA distinguished populations associated with GAL3 immunoreactivity. Imaging mass cytometry further showed that aged fimbria myeloid cells had greater GAL3, CD38, uPAR, dPP4, IBA1, and CD45 intensity than hippocampal myeloid cells, while the GAL3-stratified analysis specifically supported enrichment of uPAR and CD38, not dPP4.
Insight2.relevant: GAL3+ cells were rare in young mouse brains. In aged brains, we observed GAL3+ cells in multiple limbic regions (Extended Data Fig. 1a) with dense localization in white matter tracts, especially the fimbria (Extended Data Fig. 1a). In aged fimbria, GAL3 signal colocalized with the myeloid/microglial marker IBA1 but not with the astrocyte marker GFAP (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). GAL3 immunoreactivity comprised a larger area of old versus young female fimbria; however, GAL3 area was not significantly different in fimbria between old and young male mice (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In the old female fimbria, IBA1+GAL3+ cells were larger relative to IBA1+GAL3− cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). PCA of IBA1+GAL3+ and IBA1+GAL3− populations from old mouse fimbria revealed size-specific principal components based on cellular morphology and distinguished by GAL3+ immunoreactivity (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Thus, immunofluorescent imaging and gene expression demonstrate increased abundance of the senescent and DAM marker GAL3/Lgals3 in aged white matter, including the fimbria, which was more pronounced in aged female mice. […] Fimbria myeloid cells exhibited greater intensity of IBA1, GAL3, CD38, uPAR, dPP4 and CD45, relative to hippocampal myeloid cells, which exhibited greater CX3CR1 protein levels (Fig. 2b). Stratification of GAL3+ and GAL3− cells in the fimbria showed that GAL3+ cells harbored trending or significantly higher levels of senescence-related markers uPAR and CD38 (Fig. 2c).

Insight3.summary: GeoMx digital spatial profiling of aged female mouse brains found that established senescence- and DAM-associated genes (Fth1, Ctss, and Apoe) and candidate or emergent genes (Ccno and Sesn3) were enriched in fimbria IBA1+ microglia relative to hippocampal IBA1+ populations. Within the aged fimbria, Apoe was the most abundantly expressed transcript in IBA1+GAL3+ relative to IBA1+GAL3− microglia and strongly distinguished these populations.
Insight3.how: The authors used GeoMx whole-transcriptome spatial profiling on 5-µm FFPE sagittal sections from 28-month-old female mouse brains, selecting areas with IBA1, GAL3, and SYTO83 and using GFAP for negative selection. They compared IBA1+ populations from hippocampus and fimbria and found enrichment of Fth1, Ctss, Apoe, Ccno, and Sesn3 in fimbria IBA1+ cells. They also compared IBA1+GAL3+ and IBA1+GAL3− populations within the aged fimbria, where Apoe was the most abundantly expressed gene in the GAL3+ population relative to the GAL3− population. Differential expression was analyzed with a two-sided DESeq2 Wald test, and the authors cautioned that GeoMx DSP is useful for signature discovery but limited for molecularly phenotyping rare or heterogeneous cell populations.
Insight3.relevant: We next examined microglial transcriptional signatures specific to the hippocampus and fimbria of old female mice using GeoMx DSP. We segmented the hippocampus and fimbria regions with positive selection based on GAL3, IBA1 and SYTO83 labels and negative selection by GFAP (Fig. 3a). First, we compared IBA1+ populations in the hippocampus versus fimbria (Fig. 3b). Established senescence and DAM genes Fth1, Ctss and Apoe and candidate senescence-related genes, Ccno and Sesn3, were enriched in IBA1+ cells of the fimbria. We next compared transcriptional profiles of IBA1+GAL3+ and IBA1+GAL3− microglia specifically in aged fimbria (Fig. 3c,d). Apoe was the most abundantly expressed gene in IBA1+GAL3+ cells, relative to IBA1+GAL3− cells. We discovered conserved senescence- and DAM-associated genes (Fth1, Apoe and Ctss) and emergent genes (Ccno and Sesn3) were enriched in aged fimbria microglia. Apoe strongly distinguished GAL3+ versus GAL3− microglia in the fimbria. These experiments underscore the utility of GeoMx for expression signature discovery; however, GeoMx DSP remains limited for molecularly phenotyping rare or heterogenous cell populations.

Insight4.summary: CosMx spatial molecular imaging identified an aged-brain-exclusive microglial population in dataset 2 (cluster 10), concentrated in white matter but also present in gray matter, with canonical DAM and senescence-related gene expression and the highest SenBrain score. This population showed molecular overlap with dataset-1 cluster 7, and the senescence- and DAM-linked profile was reproducibly detected across independent datasets after Harmony integration.
Insight4.how: A 50-gene aging- and senescence-associated panel was combined with the 950-plex CosMx mouse neuroscience panel to create the 102-gene SenBrain panel. In dataset 1, cluster 7 had the highest SenBrain enrichment, the greatest frequency of Lgals3-positive cells, and increased expression of DAM-associated genes. In dataset 2, cluster 10 was present only in aged brain, concentrated in white matter, expressed canonical DAM- and senescence-related genes, and had the highest overall SenBrain score while overlapping molecularly with cluster 7. Harmony integration produced cluster 6 with concordant profiles and the highest SenBrain score, supporting reproducible senescence and DAM signatures across the two datasets.
Insight4.relevant: We used the custom panel combined with the 950-plex CosMx mouse neuroscience panel, enabling investigation of 102 senescence-related genes that we term the 'SenBrain' panel. We identified the highest enrichment of the SenBrain gene module in aged microglial cluster 7. Microglial cluster 7 harbored the greatest frequency of Lgals3+ cells. Cluster 10 was characterized by increased expression of canonical DAM- and senescence-related genes, including Apoe, Axl, Itgax, Lgals3, Lgals3bp, Lilrb4a/b, Lpl, Lyz1/2, Mmp12, Spp1 and Tyrobp. Cluster 10 also demonstrated a molecular profile overlap with the previous senescent DAM population identified in aged microglia from Fig. 4 (cluster 7). Cluster 10, which was only present in the aged brain, showed the highest overall SenBrain score. Similar to the previously described continuous nature of DAM and WAM states, this population (cluster 10) was identifiable in white and gray matter but was concentrated in white matter. Harmonized cluster 6 exhibited a gene expression profile highly concordant with cluster 7 from Fig. 4 and cluster 10 from Figs. 5 and 6. Cluster 6 displayed the highest SenBrain score and together with the combined Lgals3-enriched microglial gene set, demonstrated reproducible senescence and DAM signatures across both datasets. Therefore, the senescence- and DAM-linked microglial profile is a conserved feature of aged corticolimbic brain regions and CosMx SMI can reproducibly detect conserved microglial states across independent datasets comprising different sample sizes and distinct age groups.

Insight5.summary: Senescence transcriptional programs in aged white-matter microglia are integrated within the broader DAM continuum rather than constituting a separable microglial state. The aged-only white matter-enriched cluster 7 shows enrichment across all six SenBrain domains, while the age-exclusive cluster 10 in the young-versus-old comparison is selectively enriched for SASP, organelle stress, and cell surface domains, with nuclear stress specifically marking the distinct age-dominant cluster 3. Organelle stress and cell surface domains are shared across aged populations, and SenBrain enrichment is inversely related to homeostatic microglial identity.
Insight5.how: The SenBrain panel was parsed into six senescence domains and scored per cell using AddModuleScore. In dataset 1 (aged microglia), white matter-enriched cluster 7 demonstrated pronounced enrichment across all six senescence domains (Fig. 4m). In dataset 2 (young vs. old), the age-exclusive cluster 10 showed the highest overall SenBrain score but was specifically enriched for cell surface, organelle stress, and SASP domains, while age-dominant cluster 3 showed nuclear stress enrichment (Fig. 6d). SenBrain scores showed an inverse relationship with homeostatic microglial module enrichment (Figs. 5j, 6b,c; Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Cross-dataset harmonization confirmed a conserved senescent-DAM population (Extended Data Fig. 7j). The authors conclude that at these ages, senescence programs appear integrated with the DAM signature rather than forming a discrete subset, and that distinct senescent DAM subsets may only resolve at older ages or in neurodegenerative models.
Insight5.relevant: We parsed the SenBrain panel into senescence domains (Supplementary Table 2) and investigated the scores and percentage of cells enriched for individual modules. The white matter-enriched cluster 7 demonstrated pronounced frequency and expression enrichment across all investigated senescence domains, including cell cycle regulation, nuclear stress, SASP, senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathway (SCAP), organelle stress and cell surface markers (Fig. 4m). This corresponded to comparatively elevated expression of specific senescence-related genes, including Cdkn2d/p19ink4d (cell cycle regulation); Cenpb, Hmgb1, Pak2 and Smad2 (nuclear stress); Ccl3–4, Csf1, Mmp12 and Spp1 (SASP); Akt1 and Bcl2l1 (SCAP); Cyba, Lgals3, Lgals3bp and Lpl (organelle stress); and Axl, Cd9, Gpnmb and Plaur (cell surface markers) (Fig. 4g). … Age-exclusive cluster 10 was enriched for senescence domains including cell surface, organelle stress and SASP, implicating this population as a dominant proinflammatory microglial phenotype (Fig. 6d). Specific senescence-related genes enriched in cluster 10 included Cdkn2c/p18ink4c (cell cycle regulation); Ccl3, Ccl5, Csf1, Mmp12 and Spp1 (SASP); Cyba, Lgals3 and Lpl (organelle stress); and Axl and Gpnmb (cell surface markers). Age-dominant cluster 3 was enriched for cell surface, organelle stress and nuclear stress domains (Fig. 6d). … Organelle stress and cell surface remodeling emerged as shared senescence domains, whereas SASP and nuclear stress domains were distinctly enriched among the two age-increased populations. … For several clusters, SenBrain enrichment was inversely related to the homeostatic-associated microglia module (Figs. 5j and 6b,c and Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). … In our analysis of 24- and 4-month-old female mice, senescence-associated transcriptional programs appear integrated with the broader DAM signature. At older ages or in neurodegenerative models, senescent programs may be further amplified, revealing specific senescent DAM subsets, such as the Ccl4+ senescent population identified within DAM microglia in a mouse model of tauopathy.

Insight6.summary: Canonical senescence biomarkers are detected only sparsely and heterogeneously in aged microglia—Cdkn2a/p16 was found in just 1–5% of cells with a heterogeneous profile, and the age-exclusive senescent-DAM cluster showed only low Cdkn2c/p18ink4c—leading the authors to caution that no single marker defines senescence and that multi-biomarker, multi-domain scoring is required.
Insight6.how: Within the CosMx datasets, the authors examined all microglia expressing any Cdkn and compared them to Cdkn-negative microglia, and separately interrogated the Cdkn2a+ fraction across age groups (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Microglia expressing any Cdkn showed increased Cdkn1b, Cdkn2a, Cdkn2c, Apoe, Csf3r, Hmgb1, Tgfbr1, Cyfip1, P2ry12 and Sparc; aged versus young Cdkn2a+ microglia differed in Cdkn2a, Apoe, C1qa and Clu (up) and Trem2 and Serpine1 (down), indicating age-dependent functional divergence. Methodologically, the CosMx probes for Cdkn2a span both p16ink4a and p19arf exons, and the platform lacks signal amplification, limiting detection of low-abundance transcripts; the authors state that additional approaches are needed to conclusively map p16-positive microglial identity. The SenBrain panel description explicitly advises analysts to require a minimum of two to three distinct biomarkers and/or senescence domains, acknowledging that any individual SenBrain gene may be altered in non-senescent contexts. The authors also note that Cdkn2c/p18ink4c, which can coordinate cell-cycle arrest via CDK4/CDK6, was lowly detected even in the cluster 10 senescent DAM population.
Insight6.relevant: Among all aged microglia, we observed that the expression profiles across distinct and total Cdkn+ microglia were heterogenous (Supplementary Fig. 2). Furthermore, we detected low-level expression of multiple Cdkns across most individual microglial populations; cluster 8 harbored the highest expression (Extended Data Fig. 2j). […] Examination of the cell cycle regulation domain revealed that young and old microglia broadly and lowly expressed cell cycle regulatory markers (Extended Data Fig. 6). In examination of microglia expressing any Cdkn, the genes Cdkn1b, Cdkn2a, Cdkn2c, Apoe, Csf3r, Hmgb1, Tgfbr1, Cyfip1, P2ry12 and Sparc were increased relative to microglia without Cdkn expression (Extended Data Fig. 6a). As a top senescence biomarker, we investigated Cdkn2a+ microglia, which exhibited a heterogenous profile (Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). Across all microglial clusters, 1–5% of cells were positive for Cdkn2a. Among total aged versus young Cdkn2a+ microglia, we observed age-increased expression of Cdkn2a, Apoe, C1qa and Clu, and age-decreased expression of Trem2 and Serpine1, among other factors, suggesting distinct roles for Cdkn2a+ microglia in the aged versus young brain (Extended Data Fig. 6b). The expanded identity and impacts of cells expressing this heterogeneous, low-level expression biomarker warrant further investigation. […] Cdkn2a was lowly detected across microglial CosMx populations; however, Cdkn2a CosMx probes include p16ink4a and p19arf exons, and this probe-based method does not involve signal amplification to improve detection of lowly abundant transcripts. Thus, additional approaches are needed to conclusively map p16-positive microglial identities and impacts in the aging brain. Of note, Cdkn2c/p18ink4c, which can coordinate cell cycle arrest through interactions with CDK4 or CDK6, was lowly detected in the cluster 10 senescent DAM population. […] As a disclaimer, we encourage analysts using SenBrain or any other senescence gene list to consider a minimum of two to three distinct biomarkers and/or senescence domains… There is no single biomarker for senescence, and any biomarkers in the SenBrain list may in fact be altered in distinct brain contexts not related to senescence.

Insight7.summary: The authors converted a recognized technical artifact of spatial transcriptomics — low-level 'molecular shadow' transcripts misassigned from neighboring cells — into an analytical asset they termed molecular 'contact-tracing.' They showed that white matter-localized microglia carry spillover oligodendrocyte/myelin transcripts (Mbp, Mobp, Plp1) while gray matter-localized microglia carry neuronal spillover (Camk2a, Adcy1, Sncb, Snap25), with astrocytic markers partitioning as Aldoc (gray) versus Gfap (white); they formalized this into canonical cell-type gene-set modules that independently corroborated their anatomical cluster assignments.
Insight7.how: The authors first performed two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum differential expression between white matter- and gray matter-localized microglia (Fig. 4e), revealing region-specific enrichment of non-microglial markers interpreted as spillover from adjacent cells. They then constructed 'contact-tracing' gene-set modules for major brain cell types from published datasets (Supplementary Table 2) and scored each CosMx microglial cluster (Fig. 4j,k; Fig. 5j; Supplementary Fig. 5). In the young-versus-old dataset, clusters 2, 3, 9, 10 and 15 scored high on the oligodendrocyte module and localized to white matter; clusters 4, 7 and 14 scored high on the neuronal module and localized to gray matter; cluster 15 additionally scored on an ependymocyte module; cluster 1 scored on the microglial/homeostatic module; and cluster 13 showed enrichment for both the homeostatic and DAM modules, consistent with a transitional state. The same logic applied to non-microglial immune cells showed aged cells carrying elevated Gfap, Plp1, Mbp, Mobp and complement transcripts relative to young cells, interpreted as proximity to resident glia. The approach was confirmed with anatomical registration.
Insight7.relevant: "An inherent artifact of current single-cell spatial platforms and segmentation algorithms is low-level detection of transcripts from adjacent or interacting cells. By exploiting this signal as a variant of molecular 'contact-tracing', we observed that white matter-localized microglia were enriched for oligodendrocyte transcripts Mbp, Mobp and Plp1, whereas gray matter-localized microglia were distinctly enriched for neuronal transcripts Camk2a, Adcy1, Sncb and Snap25, indicating close proximity to, or potentially prior engulfment of these cells (Fig. 4e). Distinct astrocytic markers were enriched in gray (for example, Aldoc) and white (for example, Gfap) matter-localized microglia (Fig. 4e)." "To profile transcripts from neighboring and/or interacting cells, we devised canonical gene set modules of distinct brain cell types (Supplementary Table 2) using previously published data and interrogated the 'contact-tracing modules' and enrichment for SenBrain and DAM signatures in clusters (Fig. 4j–k). We detected enrichment for immune cell and choroid plexus related gene modules in cluster 1, 7 and 9, oligodendrocyte module in clusters 1 and 4, neuronal module in cluster 3 and astrocyte and vascular modules in cluster 9 (Fig. 4k)." "Microglial clusters 2, 3, 9, 10 and 15 exhibited higher oligodendrocyte module scores, whereas clusters 4, 7 and 14 exhibited higher neuron module scores, corroborating the white and gray matter-majority anatomical localizations (Fig. 5j, Extended Data Fig. 4c–i and Supplementary Fig. 5a). Clusters 1 and 13 were enriched for the microglia cell-type module, suggestive of homeostatic populations, whereas clusters 3, 10 and 13 were enriched for the DAM module… Cluster 15 was enriched for an ependymocyte module, suggesting proximity to ventricular borders (Fig. 5j and Supplementary Fig. 5d)." "Relative to young immune cells, higher levels of astrocyte (Gfap), oligodendrocyte (Plp1, Mbp and Mobp), and microglia (C1qa, C1qb and Ctss) markers were detected in old immune cells, suggesting proximity to brain-resident glia (Supplementary Fig. 3d)." "Current spatial mapping molecular markers and segmentation algorithms are imperfect, resulting in detection of 'molecular shadows', corresponding to low-level transcript localizations of cell identity markers that probably originate from adjacent cells rather than the segmented cell. We exploited this methodological artifact as a way of classifying spatial neighborhood characteristics of cell populations, which were confirmed with anatomical registration."

Insight8.summary: Monocle3 trajectory inference on the combined young-plus-old CosMx dataset suggests that the age-exclusive senescent-DAM population (cluster 10) can be reached by at least two anatomically distinct routes — a longer homeostatic gray-matter trajectory (1 → 13 → 3 → 10) and a more direct white-matter/ependymocyte–oligodendrocyte trajectory (8 → 15 → 3 → 10) — supporting the interpretation that microenvironmental priming, rather than a unique cellular origin, confers the convergent age-selective transcriptional signature.
Insight8.how: The authors first identified gradient increases in senescence/DAM marker expression and cell-percentage enrichment across clusters 1 → 13 → 3 → 10 (Fig. 6e). They applied Monocle3 to the integrated young+old CosMx microglia, excluding peripheral clusters unreachable from the core partition (Fig. 6f). A forward model rooted at homeostatic cluster 1 branched from cluster 3 into 9, 10, or 15 → 8 (Fig. 6g(i)); a retrograde model rooted at cluster 10 showed three precursor branches converging on it via cluster 15/8, cluster 9, and cluster 13 → 1 (Fig. 6g(ii)). The 8 → 15 → 3 → 10 route required the fewest branch points. Pseudotime distance from cluster 10 inversely correlated with SenBrain and DAM module scores. The authors interpret these convergent trajectories — alongside three non-exclusive biological scenarios — as evidence that anatomical microenvironmental context, rather than a singular lineage, shapes the common senescent-DAM transcriptional endpoint, while noting that spatially resolved lineage mapping is needed to validate these inferences.
Insight8.relevant: We next modeled fate trajectories that may give rise to age-increased microglial populations within the aged (n = 4) versus young (n = 4) dataset (Figs. 5 and 6). We examined SenBrain gene expression gradients that may indicate a trajectory from homeostatic microglia (cluster 1) toward the age-exclusive cluster 10 (Fig. 6e). Across clusters 1, 13, 3 and 10, we observed gradient increases in the percentage of cells and average expression for several senescence and DAM-associated markers, including Apoe, Axl, C4bi, Cd9, Clec7a, Ctsb, Lgals3 and Tyrobp. We applied Monocle3 trajectory inference, excluding peripheral clusters (2, 6, 11 and 12, as defined by the UMAP) that were unreachable from the main core partition (Fig. 6f). Our initial model included homeostatic cluster 1 as the pseudotime root and proceeded to cluster 13, following to 3, which then branched into 9, 10 or 15 → 8 terminal populations (Fig. 6g(i)). This 1 → 13 → 3 → 10 trajectory tracked with the age-increased transcript gradients described above (Fig. 6e) and was characterized by proportional decreases in young cell abundance (Fig. 5e(ii)). To explore alternative trajectories resulting in the age-increased populations, we interrogated a retrograde model with terminal cluster 10 as the pseudotime root (Fig. 6g(ii)). Inferred retrograde trajectories branched from cluster 10 to 3, bearing both DAM and SenBrain-enriched genes, then branched toward three trajectories: (1) ependymocyte-, astrocyte- and oligodendrocyte-associated cluster 15 and astrocyte-associated cluster 8, (2) choroid plexus and oligodendrocyte-associated cluster 9 and (3) DAM- and homeostatic-microglia-associated cluster 13 with continued branching toward neuron-associated populations, including homeostatic cluster 1 (Fig. 6g(ii)). Based on trajectory branching of subpopulations, we determined that the retrograde-inferred astrocyte-, ependymocyte- and oligodendrocyte-associated microglial trajectory involving population 15 (8 → 15 → 3 → 10) was the most direct route to cluster 10 and involved the fewest branch points, whereas the gray matter-enriched homeostatic microglial trajectory (1 → 13 → 3 → 10) contained more branch points (Fig. 6g(ii)). Pseudotime values were inversely correlated with SenBrain and DAM module scores, and the greatest pseudotime distance from cluster 10 was represented in terminal gray matter populations (Supplementary Fig. 6). The models suggest that senescent DAM cells may emerge along multiple possible molecular trajectories, probably resultant of anatomically defined microenvironment priming that ultimately confers common age-selective transcriptional signatures. Additional spatially resolved lineage mapping and cell–cell communication analyses are needed to validate lineage inferences and the context-dependent signaling networks that drive cell fate trajectories in brain aging and disease.

Insight9.summary: Systemic senescent-cell targeting partially reduced age-increased senescence and DAM gene expression in aged female white matter: pharmacogenetic ablation of p16+ cells with AP20187 lowered p16ink4a in female fimbria-fornix/corpus callosum and hippocampus and lowered Trem2, Tmem173 and Tyrobp in white matter, while both AP20187 and the BCL2-inhibitor venetoclax lowered Lgals3 in aged female FFCC — with venetoclax not reducing p16ink4a, consistent with the authors' interpretation that p16 and BCL2 targeting engage partially distinct molecular axes; male transcriptional responses were more heterogeneous.
Insight9.how: Old (16–20 month) p16-InkAttac mice were randomized by weight and age to vehicle, AP20187 (2 mg/kg i.p., which induces death of p16-expressing cells) or venetoclax (50 mg/kg oral gavage), on a regimen of five consecutive daily doses, 2 weeks off, then a second 5-day course, discontinued 1 week before necropsy; young vehicle-treated mice served as baseline. RT-PCR on microdissected FFCC and HIP was normalized to Hprt and to sex-matched young controls, and groups were compared by one-way ANOVA with exact P values versus old control (Fig. 7a–f). Sample sizes: n = 5/sex young control, n = 6F/8M old control, n = 4–5F/8M old AP20187, n = 5F/6M old venetoclax. In females, AP20187 reduced FFCC-p16ink4a (P = 0.0234), HIP-p16ink4a (P < 0.0001), FFCC-Trem2 (P = 0.0024), FFCC-Tmem173 (P = 0.0164) and FFCC-Tyrobp (P = 0.0256); AP20187 and venetoclax both reduced FFCC-Lgals3 (P = 0.0074 and P = 0.0160), but only AP20187 reduced p16ink4a. The authors note that transcriptional profiles were more heterogeneous in male mice and that larger validation cohorts are needed.
Insight9.relevant: "We next tested the hypothesis that systemic targeting of senescent cells would reduce the abundance of senescence and DAM markers in aged fimbria-fornix and corpus collosum. We treated old p16-InkAttac mice with either vehicle, AP20187, which induces cell death in p16-expressing cells, or the senolytic BCL2-inhibitor venetoclax. Young vehicle-treated mice were also assessed. AP20187 reduced p16ink4a expression in female fimbria-fornix and corpus collosum white matter (Fig. 7a) and hippocampal gray matter (Fig. 7b). AP20187 and venetoclax reduced age-increased Lgals3 in female fimbria-fornix and corpus collosum (Fig. 7c). AP20187 also reduced Trem2, Tmem173 and Tyrobp in aged female fimbria-fornix and corpus collosum (Fig. 7d–f). Transcriptional profiles were more heterogenous in male mice (Fig. 7)." "BCL2 targeting also reduced DAM markers but not Cdkn2a/p16ink4a expression, and Bcl2 was detected in microglial cluster 13, which was proportionally enriched in the aged brain. Contextualized with trajectory analyses, senolytic strategies may target cells tracking toward the terminal age-increased dominant SenBrain-high senotype." "Our expression profiling and immunofluorescent imaging demonstrate that systemic p16 targeting reduces senescence and DAM markers in aged white matter. Additional validation of p16-InkAttac targeting with larger sample sizes are needed to identify the full efficacy of aged phenotype reversal." "Old p16-InkAttac mice were randomized (based on body weight and age, 16–20 months old) to receive vehicle, AP20187 (2 mg kg−1, i.p. injection) or venetoclax (50 mg kg−1) by oral gavage. … Mice received five consecutive daily administrations for 1 week, 2 weeks off and then another 5-day treatment. Treatments were discontinued 1 week before necropsy."

Insight10.summary: Senotherapeutics partially reverted the aged fimbria microglial phenotype toward a youthful state at cellular and tissue-architectural levels — reducing IBA1+ density and cell size, restoring youth-like alignment of microglia to fiber tracts, and lowering GAL3+ and APOE+ burden — with AP20187 and venetoclax converging on GAL3+ microglia through distinct effector routes (AP20187 reducing per-cell GAL3 intensity; venetoclax reducing IBA1+GAL3+ cell number without altering residual intensity). The authors posit that the fimbria's anatomical adjacency to the choroid plexus and lateral ventricle underlies both its selective age-related vulnerability and its responsiveness to systemic senotherapy, while cautioning that the same regimens alter young fimbria microglia, limiting translational application in young organisms.
Insight10.how: Using the opposite hemisphere from the gene-expression cohort (Fig. 7), the authors quantified IBA1+ immunofluorescence in young and old vehicle-, AP20187- and venetoclax-treated p16-InkAttac female fimbria (Fig. 8a–e). IBA1+ density was higher in old than young fimbria and was returned to youthful levels by AP20187 (P = 0.0095); both drugs reduced IBA1+ cell size (P = 0.0045, P = 0.0003) (Fig. 8b,c). Microglial alignment to DAPI-estimated fiber tracts (long-axis angular offset of each IBA1+ cell's Feret axis to the nearest tract) showed greater alignment in old versus young mice, and AP20187 shifted the distribution toward youth-like organization (Kolmogorov–Smirnov P < 0.001 for both comparisons) (Fig. 8d). A published microglial phenotyping composite index (cell area, convex hull area/density, perimeters, span ratio, Feret length, tract-angle offset, circularity) plus PCA separated old control microglia from young, old AP20187 and old venetoclax, with AP20187 cells shifting toward young profiles and venetoclax cells clustering by increased circularity and decreased size (Fig. 8e). Both drugs reduced GAL3 footprint and the frequency of IBA1+GAL3+ cells (Fig. 8f,g); AP20187 additionally lowered per-cell GAL3 intensity in remaining GAL3+ cells (KS P < 0.001), whereas venetoclax reduced cell number without altering residual intensity — interpreted as "distinct effector populations… converge on GAL3+ microglia" (Fig. 8h; Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). APOE immunofluorescence intensity and APOE/GAL3 colocalization were reduced by both drugs (Fig. 8i–l), and treated mice showed more dispersed APOE+ cell organization relative to the fimbria midline (Fig. 8m; Extended Data Fig. 9). The authors caution that the same regimens altered young fimbria microglia (venetoclax reduced IBA1+ abundance; both drugs increased cell size and reduced density), corresponding to low Cdkn2a and Bcl2 detection in young brain, limiting senolytic application in young organisms. They further posit that the fimbria's spatial adjunction to choroid plexus and lateral ventricle exposes it to circulating factors and infiltrating immune cells, potentially explaining both its aging vulnerability and its responsiveness to systemic senotherapy.
